extracted.intended_audience: company executives, founders, in-house and outside securities counsel, underwriters, and other stakeholders preparing for or advising on an IPO (also useful for investors wanting to understand the rules)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and compliance rules for corporate communications before, during, and immediately after an IPO (the SEC 'quiet period'), including phase-specific restrictions, required paperwork, internal policies, and enforcement risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quiet period — definition and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The quiet period is a set timeframe when a company planning to issue new securities is legally restricted by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) from making public statements that could be seen as promoting or 'hyping' the sale. Its purpose is to level the playing field and ensure investors rely on the vetted information in the prospectus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think of it as a federally mandated 'cone of silence' that prevents selective hype and conditions the market; communications must be controlled to avoid 'gun-jumping.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal foundation: Section 5 and the three statutory phases
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 5 of the Securities Act of 1933 divides the IPO process into three phases (Pre-Filing, Waiting/Cooling-Off, and Post-Effective) with different communication rules, even though the phrase 'quiet period' does not appear in the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand which statutory phase you are in before making any public statements; the applicable phase determines what communications are permitted or forbidden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-Filing Period restrictions (The 'True Quiet')
rubrics_metrics.description: Before filing Form S-1, the company cannot make any 'offers' to sell the securities — the SEC interprets 'offer' broadly to include communications that might arouse public interest in the stock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What's forbidden: announcing the IPO before filing, interviews about the company's future, overly optimistic press releases, new high-profile ad campaigns. What's allowed: ordinary-course business communications (factual product announcements, ongoing advertising), required factual financial disclosures. Bottom line: apply the intent/effect test — if the communication is designed to get people excited about buying stock, it risks being gun-jumping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiting/Cooling-Off Period rules
rubrics_metrics.description: From filing the S-1 until the registration is declared 'effective,' written offers are limited to the formal preliminary prospectus (the 'red herring'); oral offers (roadshows) are permitted, but promotional media interviews and forecasts remain prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowed activities: distributing the red herring to potential investors, conducting roadshows (oral offers), and — for Emerging Growth Companies (EGCs) under the JOBS Act — 'testing the waters' with qualified investors. Forbidden: selling securities and distributing written sales material other than the preliminary prospectus, making projections not included in the filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-Effective Period and underwriter quiet (initial post-IPO window)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the SEC declares the registration effective, the stock can be sold; however, underwriters are subject to a restricted period (now typically 10 days) during which they are limited in publishing research reports and making 'buy' recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the initial window ends, analysts and executives can speak more freely — but all communications remain subject to other securities laws and disclosure obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gun-jumping prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: Gun-jumping is the illegal act of conditioning the market by making promotional statements or offers to sell securities before the registration statement is effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences include SEC enforcement (delays, required S-1 amendments, fines) and potential investor claims; use conservative review processes to avoid inadvertent gun-jumping.

rubrics_metrics.name: JOBS Act / EGC 'testing the waters' allowance
rubrics_metrics.description: The JOBS Act created 'Emerging Growth Companies' (EGCs) and permitted them to 'test the waters' by communicating with certain sophisticated investors before filing an S-1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a limited exemption: companies may have private meetings with Qualified Institutional Buyers and Institutional Accredited Investors to gauge interest, but public promotional communications remain restricted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish a formal written communications policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Before beginning the IPO process, the company should adopt a clear, written policy that defines the start and end of the quiet period, designates authorized spokespeople, and establishes procedures for reviewing all communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The policy should designate a small group (e.g., CEO, CFO, General Counsel) authorized to speak, set review requirements for press releases, blog posts, social media, and internal memos, and provide clear 'do's and don'ts' for employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory training for all employees
rubrics_metrics.description: Every employee — from senior executives to interns — must receive training on quiet period rules and the company's communication policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training should cover what the quiet period is and why it matters, specific prohibitions on forecasting and hyping the offering, and the company's process for handling inquiries from media, investors, family, and friends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutinize and control public-facing content
rubrics_metrics.description: During the quiet period, review and control all external content (website, social media, press releases, advertising) to ensure it is factual and historical rather than forward-looking or promotional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical steps: review the website for forward-looking language, lock down corporate social media accounts, instruct employees not to post about performance or plans, adopt a blanket 'no comment' on IPO-related inquiries, and route all media or investor inquiries to legal/communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration Statement (Form S-1) and prospectus obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Form S-1 is the master registration document filed with the SEC and contains the prospectus, which must include an exhaustive description of the business, risk factors, financial statements, and management information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preliminary prospectus ('red herring') may be distributed during the waiting period; the final prospectus must accompany sales. Treat the S-1 as the single source of truth for the offering and ensure other communications do not contradict or supplement it in an unfiled manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free Writing Prospectus (FWP) rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A free writing prospectus is any written communication outside the official prospectus that offers to sell the security; FWPs can provide additional information but are subject to complex rules and filing requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using a free writing prospectus, ensure it complies with SEC filing requirements and is coordinated with counsel and underwriters to avoid inadvertent distribution of unfiled promotional material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent and effect test for communications
rubrics_metrics.description: The practical test for whether a communication violates quiet period rules is its intent and effect: is it part of normal business, or is it designed to condition the market and arouse interest in buying stock?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this test conservatively. Even seemingly innocuous communications can be problematic if they have the effect of promoting the offering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media and modern communication risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Social media activity (tweets, posts, likes) by executives or company accounts can be treated as offers or promotional statements under the same rules that apply to traditional media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lock down corporate and executive social accounts during the quiet period, include social media guidance in training, and route any online inquiries to legal. Be aware policing is difficult and the SEC has confirmed social media falls within the rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different types of 'quiet periods' and their rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all 'quiet periods' are IPO quiet periods: e.g., M&A quiet periods (confidentiality to prevent leaks/insider trading) and post-earnings quiet periods (self-imposed to avoid selective disclosure) have different purposes and rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which kind of quiet period applies in any situation and apply the specific restrictions relevant to that context rather than assuming IPO rules apply universally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Players and their responsibilities (issuer, underwriters, SEC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Key actors include the issuing company (and its executives), the underwriters (investment banks), and the SEC. Underwriters are jointly liable for quiet period violations and must follow their own restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure coordination among issuer, counsel, and underwriters; train executives; recognize underwriters face their own research/publication restrictions (e.g., the initial 10-day research blackout).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and enforcement (case-study lessons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations can lead to required S-1 amendments, IPO delays, SEC enforcement actions, fines, and reputational harm (illustrated by Google and Salesforce examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use case studies (Google's Playboy interview, Salesforce's NYT profile) to emphasize that even large companies can suffer severe consequences; adopt conservative practices and counsel review to mitigate risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: How alternative capital-raising models affect quiet period application
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct listings and SPAC transactions change the application of quiet-period rules because they differ structurally from traditional IPO offerings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In direct listings the quiet period may apply differently because there's no traditional new-offering prospectus; SPAC structures create separate communication regimes — get targeted legal advice for alternative routes to public markets.
